schools.summary: Henry reads Michtam as a golden psalm, precious above fine gold, because it speaks so plainly of Christ and his resurrection; Spurgeon takes 'preserve me' as 'guard me,' the manhood of Jesus needing preservation and the elect preserved in his preservation.

Clarke canvasses the title (Chaldee 'straight sculpture,' LXX 'inscription on a pillar,' michtam = stamped gold) yet doubts such meanings; reads the prayer as the man Christ Jesus in Gethsemane, El the strong God suited to a frail humanity.

Gill: prayer proper to Christ as man, heard in his preservation from Herod and in the wilderness; Calvin weighs the golden-letters and durable-pillar views of Michtam but inclines to take it for some kind of tune or melody.

Ellicott renders 'for I have found refuge in thee' (Ps. 7:1), the verb a preterite; Keil and Delitzsch infer David from the compressed, antiquated language — a friend of God in danger of death, yet without gloomy struggle.
Augustine hears the King speaking in the character of the human nature He assumed, whose royal title was set forth at his passion.

sides.position: a golden psalm (michtam = stamped/pure gold), worthy to be written in letters of gold
an inscription engraved on a durable pillar or monument for everlasting remembrance (LXX stelographia)
a musical term — some kind of tune or melody

themes: the prayer of Christ as man
in thee do I put my trust

schools.summary: Gill takes 'O my soul, thou hast said' for an apostrophe of Christ to his own soul, the supplied words warranted by the Targum, Jarchi, Aben Ezra, and Kimchi.

Clarke reads 'Thou art my Lord' as Adonai, my prop and stay, and 'my goodness' as 'my bounty,' which adds nothing to the divinity but extends to the saints; Wesley: 'thou dost not need me or my service.'
Spurgeon hears the Lord Jesus vowing allegiance for our sakes, the work of redemption not needful on account of any necessity in the Divine Being.

Ellicott calls the passage exceedingly corrupt: the versions favour 'I said' over 'thou hast said' ('O my soul' a Chaldee gloss), yielding 'I have no good besides thee' — 'my good' being happiness, not conduct.

debates.question: What does 'my goodness extendeth not to thee' mean, and does the soul or the poet speak?

sides.position: man's goodness or service adds nothing to God (received 'thou hast said')
'I have no good besides thee' — the poet's happiness, not his conduct; read 'I said' for 'thou hast said'

themes: my goodness extendeth not to thee

schools.summary: Gill: the saints 'in the earth' are set apart in election, expiated by Christ's blood, sanctified by the Spirit; 'in the earth' marks their scattered abode, or parts them from the angels also called saints (Aben Ezra).
Henry calls them the excellent ones, God's jewels and peculiar treasure, made excellent by grace, in whom all who take the Lord for their God delight because they bear his image.

Clarke fixes the addirey (noble ones inheriting the promises) and kedoshim (the consecrated, perhaps the apostles); Wesley reads a singular love borne to all saints, but judges it fits David better than Christ.
Ellicott emends to a single sentence, 'and of the saints who are in the earth, they are the excellent in whom is all my delight.'
Augustine hears 'the saints who are on His earth' as citizens of the heavenly Jerusalem, their hope fixed by an anchor though yet conversant in the flesh.

outliers.note: Judges that the verse 'more properly agrees to David than to Christ, whose goodness was principally designed for, and imparted to, sinners' — an early sounding of the David/Messiah question.

schools.summary: Gill refers the multiplied sorrows to the idolaters themselves, not (with Aben Ezra) to the saints grieved by their idolatry.

Henry: those who multiply gods multiply griefs — one God thought too little, and hundreds not enough; the drink-offerings of blood he abhors, forbidden at God's altar but prescribed by the devil to teach cruelty.

Clarke notes no Hebrew word for God, so 'another' may be another Messiah — the unbelieving Jews, sorrows multiplied eighteen centuries; Wesley keeps the plainer Gentile idol-worship, whose blood the heathen drank.

Ellicott, with slight repointing, reads 'they shall multiply their sorrows who change to another god,' detecting the prophetic figure of idolatry as adultery (Gen. 3:16) and the rites of Moloch and Chemosh; names avoided as with baal/bosheth (Exod. 23:13).

debates.question: Is the warning aimed at literal idolaters or at the unbelieving Jews?

sides.position: literal idolaters and their bloody altars
the unbelieving nation still hastening after another Messiah

schools.summary: Gill: spoken by Christ the priest, in allusion to the Levitical priests who had no inheritance but the Lord himself — his goodness and happiness as man lay in God.

Clarke makes the Messiah speaker, given the lot to redeem mankind and the cup of suffering to impart the cup of consolation; Wesley reads a plainer contentment, the cup as the portion allotted at ancient feasts.

Ellicott ties it to the Levitical portion (Num. 18:20), the poet exiled from Canaan consoled by the better part (Savonarola, Paul); Keil and Delitzsch: the measuring lines fall where property is assigned (Micah 2:5; Josh. 17:5), God's fellowship a paradisaic possession.

debates.question: Who speaks the verse, and what does 'thou maintainest my lot' say?

sides.position: the Messiah who takes God for his portion
the exiled David consoling himself with the inheritance that cannot be lost

outliers.note: Reports Hitzig's plausible conjecture, tomid for tomikh, which would yield 'thou art ever my lot' in place of 'thou maintainest my lot.'

themes: the LORD my portion and cup

schools.summary: Gill turns the pleasant places from ground to people — the elect church given to Christ as his portion — though he allows Aben Ezra and Kimchi supply 'places.'

Clarke keeps the Messianic key — 'a rich inheritance of immortal spirits,' a Church who shall dwell with him for ever; Wesley reads a land flowing with milk and honey, blessed above all with the presence of God.
Ellicott explains the figure: the measuring cords 'fall' because the portions were distributed by lot (Josh. 17:5; Micah 2:5).

Spurgeon opens the verse into the Redeemer's joy in obedience — 'I delight to do thy will' — content with his blood-bought portion, poorer than we yet never murmuring; all saints may use the language.

outliers.note: Reads 'pleasant places' as pleasant persons — the elect church in whom Christ's portion lies — rather than tracts of ground, against the others who keep the geographical sense.

themes: the lines fallen in pleasant places

schools.summary: Gill: thanksgiving, like prayer, belongs to Christ as man and Mediator, who praises God for counsel and instruction.
Henry: counsel given by word and Spirit, while the reins — the conscience (Jer. 17:10) — instructed him in the night-season, catechizing and quickening him to live as one who had God for his portion.

Clarke: Jesus as man received all wisdom from God (Luke 2:40-52), the reins the most secret workings devoted to God, the 'night seasons' the time of the passion; Wesley: the inward thoughts moved by the Spirit, the mind working on God while others sleep.

Ellicott: 'given me counsel' = led to a happy choice, 'instruct me' better 'warn me,' conscience echoing God's voice as a binding law; Keil and Delitzsch see the closing strophe rising like seven rays of light toward a prospect that need not fear death.

themes: the reins instruct in the night

schools.summary: Henry: all these verses Peter quotes of Christ and his resurrection (Acts 2:25-28); three things bore Christ up — his Father's will, his presence at the right hand (Luke 22:43), and the joy set before him (Heb. 12:2); Spurgeon hears the fear of death overcome by a continued eye to Jehovah.
Gill: 'set the Lord always before me' is not the fear of God or the law (Jarchi) but the Lord himself, on whom Christ kept his eye, aiming always at his Father's glory.

Clarke: applied by Peter to Christ's death and resurrection, God's presence and support at his right hand keeping him from swerving; Wesley marks the seam — David spoke of himself, but from here is transported by the spirit of prophecy to speak as a type of Christ.

Ellicott reads 'at my right hand' as a military image — the shield of the right-hand comrade protecting the man beside him (Ps. 121:5); Keil and Delitzsch hear a real David whose believing confidence the promise fulfils.

debates.question: How much of vv.8-11 is David's own voice, and where does prophecy of Christ begin?

sides.position: of Christ throughout — David the prophet speaking of the Messiah's resurrection
David speaks first of himself, then is caught up from this verse to speak as a type of Christ
primarily David's own believing confidence as a friend of God, fulfilled and applied to Christ in the NT

themes: I have set the LORD always before me
he is at my right hand

schools.summary: Gill reads 'my heart is glad' of an inward joy and fulness, the same as rejoicing in spirit, because of the Lord's presence.

Clarke takes 'my glory' for the tongue (Ps. 57:8; Acts 2:26), though 'soul bids as fair,' and insists 'my flesh shall rest in hope' can in no sense be said of David — a dying Messiah's certainty of a swift resurrection (Acts 2:31); Wesley likewise makes 'glory' the tongue and the flesh's hope figurative (Rom. 8:19).

Ellicott suspects khabed (liver/heart) for khabod (glory), the LXX 'tongue' a paraphrase, heart-soul-flesh comprising the whole man (1 Thess. 5:23); 'rest in hope' truly 'rest in security,' immortality present only as a faint, unconscious ray.

sides.position: the tongue (so the LXX, quoted in Acts 2:26)
the liver or heart (khabed), the whole man in heart, soul, and flesh

debates.question: Can 'my flesh shall rest in hope' be spoken of David, or of Christ only?

sides.position: of Christ only — no sense in which it fits David; a dying Messiah's certainty of a swift resurrection
the living confidence of a soul secure in God ('rest in security'), immortality only faintly in view

themes: my flesh shall rest in hope
rest in hope or in security

schools.summary: Gill clears away the place of the damned (Christ that day in paradise); sheol/hades may mean the state of the dead, but he judges it best interpreted as the grave, 'my soul' being Christ himself or his dead body, laid there but not left.

Clarke: sheol a pit, ditch, grave, or state of the dead, to leave the soul there being to let the Messiah's life continue under death; all men see corruption but the sinless body of Christ none; the plural 'Holy One' a corruption for the singular (264 MSS, the versions, Acts 2:27; 13:35). Wesley glosses 'hell' as the state of the dead, the Holy One a title peculiar to Christ.

Ellicott: 'leave' rather 'commit,' 'hell' the unseen world (Sheol), 'Holy One' better 'thy chosen/beloved One' (chasid), the received plural's sign superfluous; 'corruption' (shachath) properly a pit (Ps. 7:15) — yet the first faint scintillation of immortality, justifying the NT use.

debates.question: What is the 'hell' (sheol) into which the soul is not left?

sides.position: the grave, from which the body was raised undecayed
the separate state of the dead, the unseen world of souls (hades/Sheol)
not the place of the damned (expressly denied)

debates.question: Is 'thine Holy One' plural or singular in the true text?

sides.position: singular (thy Holy/beloved One) — best attested by MSS, versions, and the apostolic citations (Acts 2:27; 13:35)
the received Masoretic plural, its plural-sign marked superfluous — a corruption or emphatic singular
holders: the Masoretic text (as reported by Clarke)

outliers.note: Reads 'corruption' (shachath) not as decay but as 'the pit,' so that 'to see the pit' is simply 'to die' — where Gill, Clarke, and Wesley take it of the body's corruption, from which Christ's sinless flesh was exempt.

themes: thou wilt not leave my soul in hell

schools.summary: Gill: 'the path of life' is not the way of salvation (Christ himself) but the resurrection of the dead, shown to Christ in fact by his being raised — the first-fruits and firstborn from the dead, first to tread the path to an immortal life.

Clarke: 'the way out of the regions of death, to die no more,' the plural 'life' restoring body and soul, 'thy faces' the beatific vision (1 John 3:2), netzach an onward eternal progression; Wesley paraphrases throughout of resurrection, heavenly paradise, and the right hand where Christ sits (Ps. 110:1).

Henry hears Christ's recompense for his sufferings — shown the path of life, received into God's presence and set at his right hand — yet adds that, Christ being the head, the verses belong also to all Christians animated by his Spirit.

Ellicott restores the triplet and reads 'another image for the happiness of being with God,' the larger hope only a ray faintly triumphing over death — first the settled peace of a soul that possesses God.

debates.question: Is 'the path of life' the resurrection of Christ, or the happiness of being with God?

sides.position: the resurrection of Christ that Peter and Paul proclaimed — David's tomb remaining, Christ's not
the happiness of being with God, upon which the light of immortality has only begun to break

themes: thou wilt shew me the path of life
resurrection or the presence of God
